name: High-temperature or high-light exposure
summary: Measured high temperature or unusually intense light can alter Cannabis physiology, yield, and flowering development, but published Cannabis experiments do not validate cupping, bleaching, or a single PPFD or temperature value as a universal visible injury diagnosis.
affectedParts: canopy nearest a local heat or light source
indicators: Air temperature, leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, and humidity are recorded at the affected canopy position across time
Abnormal new inflorescence clusters develop on top of older inflorescences during sustained high-temperature flowering exposure
Flower maturation or production differs from a matched cultivar under a cooler measured regime
Gas-exchange or chlorophyll-fluorescence measurements change even when a specific foliar lesion is absent
A spatial gradient repeats with measured temperature or irradiance rather than merely with leaf age
exclusions: No time-stamped canopy-level temperature, leaf-temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, or humidity record supports an exposure event
Only upward leaf curl, pale tissue, dry margins, or canopy posture is visible
Mites, thrips, webbing, cast skins, eggs, frass, or feeding scars are present
Root-zone water content, irrigation history, pH, EC, or root disease explains the distribution better
The change follows nutrient, pesticide, growth-regulator, or other chemical application
Only late-flower senescence or cultivar-typical inflorescence architecture is visible
High PPFD alone is treated as injury even though the plant is acclimated and temperature and water status are within its measured response range

progression.description: Record canopy and leaf temperature, PPFD, photoperiod, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, irrigation status, cultivar, and exact duration before assigning an environmental-exposure label.

Photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency can change with temperature; controlled Cannabis results show that the direction and optimum are variety dependent and may precede a specific visible lesion.

At 31/27 degrees Celsius day/night versus 25/21 degrees Celsius in one controlled study, abnormal new clusters developed atop older inflorescences and normal maturation was disrupted; dry-matter response differed between the two genotypes.

Compare new leaves and inflorescences after the measured exposure is corrected; persistent or spreading changes without a matching environmental gradient require renewed pest, pathogen, root-zone, nutrition, and genetic evaluation.

lookAlikes: Water shortage or excessive vapor demand
High root-zone EC or pH-related nutrient unavailability
confirmation: Map PPFD and air temperature at multiple canopy positions and times; measure leaf temperature with a calibrated contact or infrared method and record humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, photoperiod, carbon dioxide, and lamp distance.
Compare affected and unaffected plants of the same cultivar, developmental stage, irrigation treatment, and root-zone condition; include a cooler or lower-exposure reference when available.
Inspect leaf undersides and protected new growth with magnification for mites and thrips, and document the root system, substrate water content, pH, and EC.
Use serial whole-plant, canopy, and close-up images with an exposure log; do not convert a single photograph or uncalibrated camera color shift into heat- or light-stress ground truth.

For abnormal flowering, inspect multiple inflorescences over time and compare with cultivar records to separate heat-associated reversion or foxtailing from normal architecture, late-flower growth, or genetic traits.
immediateActions: Preserve the pre-correction environmental log and matched photographs, then remove an acute unsafe heat load or equipment fault gradually.
Verify irrigation delivery and root-zone moisture before changing light, humidity, or irrigation together.
Quarantine or isolate only when pest or infectious disease evidence warrants it; environmental exposure alone is not contagious.
correctivePlan: Correct the measured source, such as a canopy hot spot, failed cooling or air mixing, excessive lamp proximity, or an abrupt unacclimated light increase, while changing one controllable factor at a time.
Re-map the canopy after correction and score only new tissue and subsequent inflorescence development against a matched control.
Escalate persistent abnormalities to pest microscopy, root-zone testing, tissue analysis, or a plant diagnostic laboratory rather than repeatedly reducing light without evidence.
prevention: Log canopy-level PPFD, photoperiod, air and leaf temperature, humidity or vapor-pressure deficit, carbon dioxide, and irrigation status by zone.
Map hot spots and irradiance gradients after fixture, HVAC, canopy-height, or density changes.
Retain cultivar- and stage-matched healthy reference sequences because published temperature optima and production responses vary among Cannabis genotypes.
warnings: Upward curl, tacoing, bleaching, pale tops, dry margins, and leaf angle are nonspecific and are not validated Cannabis heat- or light-stress ground truth without measured exposure and exclusion checks.

A controlled Stillwater trial produced linearly increasing inflorescence yield through 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second; therefore PPFD magnitude alone does not prove injury or define a universal damaging threshold.
Temperature optima for photosynthesis differed among tested drug- and fiber-type varieties, so 25, 30, 35, or 40 degrees Celsius must not be generalized into one cultivar-independent diagnosis.
The abnormal inflorescence-cluster observation came from defined 31/27 degrees Celsius flowering treatments in two genotypes and should be labeled treatment-associated, not universally heat-specific.
No reusable Cannabis symptom photograph with exposure measurements and adequate causal confirmation was admitted in this record; media remain empty rather than promoting anecdotal or vendor imagery.

sources.title: High air temperature reduces plant specialized metabolite yield in medical cannabis, and has genotype-specific effects on inflorescence dry matter production
sources.organization: Environmental and Experimental Botany (Holweg et al.)
supportedClaims: In controlled short-day production, plants of two medical Cannabis genotypes were compared at 25/21 and 31/27 degrees Celsius day/night temperatures and at PPFDs of 600, 900, and 1,200 micromoles per square metre per second.

The higher-temperature treatment reduced total cannabinoid concentration in both genotypes but reduced inflorescence dry matter only in Harmony CBD, demonstrating a genotype-specific production response.

High temperature produced abnormal new inflorescence clusters on top of older inflorescences and disrupted normal maturation; this flowering morphology is treatment-associated but is not a universal image-only heat threshold.

sources.title: Temperature response of photosynthesis in different drug and fiber varieties of Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants (Chandra et al.)
sources.publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Prof. H. S. Srivastava Foundation for Science and Society
supportedClaims: Across three drug-type and four fiber-type Cannabis varieties measured from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius, photosynthetic optima varied by variety from about 25 to 35 degrees Celsius.

Dark respiration approximately doubled from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius in all tested varieties, while photosynthesis, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency showed variety-dependent responses.
The experiment measured gas exchange rather than a validated visible heat-injury syndrome, so its temperature values must not be used as universal image-label thresholds.

sources.title: Cannabis Yield, Potency, and Leaf Photosynthesis Respond Differently to Increasing Light Levels in an Indoor Environment
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Rodriguez-Morrison et al.)
supportedClaims: Indoor-grown Cannabis sativa Stillwater was exposed during flowering to average canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.
Dry inflorescence yield increased linearly through the highest tested PPFD even though leaf-level photosynthesis saturated below 1,800 micromoles per square metre per second.

The high-light experiment did not establish a universal PPFD injury threshold or validate cupping, bleaching, or edge necrosis as light-specific visual symptoms; light exposure must be interpreted with cultivar, acclimation, canopy position, temperature, carbon dioxide, and water status.

In Stillwater during the 12-hour flowering phase, chlorophyll-content index was higher in week 1 than weeks 5 and 9 and was consistently higher in upper- than lower-canopy fan leaves; the authors described evidence of early senescence but stated that the contributions of leaf age and plant ontogeny to diminished week-9 photosynthesis were unresolved.
The study measured chlorophyll index and physiology rather than validating a yellow-leaf appearance, harvest date, or universal late-flower-fade sequence.
